intro: In the middle of the 1970s, skateboarding left the sidewalk and went looking for curves. Skaters in Southern California found them in empty backyard pools. New urethane wheels and smooth bearings let them grip the walls and climb toward the coping. In 1976 the first concrete skateparks opened, and by the end of the decade there were dozens of them.

Then the parks began to close, and skaters had to find new places to ride. They built wooden ramps in backyards and turned to the street. A no-hands jump from Florida, the ollie, moved from ramp walls to flat ground. Videos on tape and new magazines carried each new trick across the country.

In this unit you will learn the people, places and dates of the pool and park years and the 1980s. You will name the parts of a pool and a ramp. You will use real physics to explain why a skater feels heavy in a curve, how height becomes speed, and how an ollie pops a board into the air.
bigQuestion: How did empty pools, new wheels and one no-hands trick change where people skate and what they can do?

title: Pools, Parks and the Ollie

chapters.title: Empty Pools and the First Skateparks
chapters.bigQuestion: How did empty swimming pools and new wheels lead to the first skateparks, and why did so many of those parks close?

story.title: A Wave Made of Concrete
story.kicker: In a dry summer in Southern California, a skater looks into an empty pool and sees a wave that never stops.
paragraphs: The summer is hot and dry in Southern California. A teenage skater climbs a backyard fence with a board under one arm. The family who owns the house has drained their pool. There is no water to fill it again, so it sits empty and quiet in the sun.

The skater kneels at the edge and looks down. The pool is shaped like a kidney bean. The flat floor of the deep end curves up into a smooth wall. At the top of the wall is a strip of blue tile and then a rounded stone lip. To a surfer, that curve looks like the face of a wave.

The skater climbs down the steps in the shallow end. They push off and roll toward the deep end. The board picks up speed on the slope. At the bottom, the wall rises ahead. They lean, carve up the curve, and feel the wheels grip the concrete. Near the tile the board slows, turns, and rolls back down.

Each run climbs a little higher. Soon the wheels are almost touching the tile. The skater is riding a wave made of concrete, and it never breaks. Across the region, other skaters are finding empty pools too. What they learn in those pools will soon be poured into the first skateparks.
story.think: Why would a surfer look at the curved wall of an empty pool and think of a wave?

lessons.title: Backyard Pools in California
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1970s, skaters in Southern California rode empty backyard pools because their smooth curved walls felt like waves.
reading: Southern California has many backyard swimming pools. Many were built after World War II, when the area grew fast. Pools from that time often had rounded shapes, like a kidney bean or a figure eight. Their floors curved smoothly up into the walls. That curve is what drew skaters.

Some skaters were riding empty pools even before the 1970s. Then came the *drought* of 1976 and 1977. A drought is a long time with much less rain than normal. Water was scarce, so some owners drained their pools or left them empty. Skaters went looking for them. They called this *pool riding*.

Many of these skaters were surfers first. The Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice had shown a low, surf-style way to skate at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975. Its riders included Peggy Oki, Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta. In pools, that style could climb walls. Skating an empty pool without the owner's permission was trespassing, and that is part of this history too.

words.d: a long period with much less rain than normal
skateboarding in an empty swimming pool, using its curved walls like a wave
going onto someone else's property without permission

The second is shaped like a kidney bean, and its floor bends in a smooth curve up into the wall. Roll a ball toward each wall. In the first pool, the ball hits the corner and bounces back. In the second, the ball rolls up the curve and back down.

choices: a long period with much less rain than normal
a deep end of a swimming pool
a contest held in a pool
check.why: A drought is a long dry period. The drought of 1976 and 1977 left many California pools empty.

check.why: A rounded pool's floor bends into its wall, so a board can roll up the curve like a wave.

check.q: Which group showed a low, surf-style way of skating at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975?
check.why: The Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice skated at Del Mar in 1975. The Bones Brigade came later.

lessons.title: The Parts of a Pool
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters learned names for each part of a pool: the flat bottom, the curved transition, the vertical wall, the tile and the coping.
reading: A pool gave skaters a new set of words. The flat floor at the bottom is the *flat bottom*. The curved part where the floor bends up into the wall is the *transition*, often called tranny for short. Above the transition, the wall can become straight up and down. Skaters call that part *vert*, short for vertical.

At the top of a pool wall is a band of tile. Above the tile is the *coping*. In a pool, coping is the rounded stone or concrete lip along the edge. Skaters learned to ride up until their wheels touched the tile. Later they rolled their back truck onto the coping and let it grind along the edge.

Pools also have a shallow end and a deep end. The deep end has the tallest walls, so it is where the biggest moves happen. The shallow end often has steps. Skaters used the steps to climb in and out. These same words, from transition to coping, are still used in every skatepark today.

words.d: the curved part of a ramp or pool where the flat floor bends up into the wall
short for vertical; the part of a wall that goes straight up and down
the rounded lip along the top edge of a pool or ramp
the flat floor at the bottom of a pool or ramp

look.title: A Pool Wall From the Side
look.text: Imagine cutting a pool in half and looking at the deep end from the side. At the bottom is a flat line: the flat bottom. Then the line bends upward in a smooth curve: the transition. Near the top, the curve stands straight up for a short way: the vert. Last comes a strip of tile and, on top, a rounded lip: the coping.
look.prompt: Trace the wall with your finger from the floor to the top. Name each part as you pass it.

the rounded lip on the edge

check.why: The transition is the curve between the flat floor and the wall.

check.why: Coping is the rounded lip at the very top of the wall, above the tile.

check.q: Why did the biggest moves happen in the deep end?

check.why: The deep end has the tallest walls, so skaters can ride higher there.

lessons.title: Wheels and Bearings That Grip
lessons.mainIdea: Urethane wheels and sealed precision bearings made it possible to grip a curved wall and roll smoothly up it.
reading: In the 1960s, most skateboard wheels were made of clay or metal. They were hard and slippery. On a curved wall, they would skid out. In the early 1970s, Frank Nasworthy began selling wheels made of *urethane*, a tough, rubbery plastic. His company was called Cadillac Wheels.

Urethane wheels grip the ground much better than clay. They also roll over small cracks and pebbles instead of stopping short. That grip comes from *friction*, the force that pushes against sliding between two surfaces. With more grip, a skater could lean into a turn on a steep wall and the wheels would hold.

In the mid-1970s, sealed precision bearings came to skateboards. A bearing is a ring of small steel balls inside each wheel that lets the wheel spin smoothly on the axle. Sealed bearings kept out dirt and rolled with less loss. Together, grippy wheels and smooth bearings let skaters carry speed up the walls of a pool.

words.d: a tough, rubbery plastic used for skateboard wheels since the early 1970s
a force that pushes against sliding between two surfaces that touch
a ring of small steel balls inside a wheel that lets it spin smoothly on the axle

look.title: Clay Wheel, Urethane Wheel
look.text: Picture two boards rolling toward the same curved wall. The first has hard clay wheels. As it starts up the curve and the rider leans, the wheels skid sideways and the board slips out. The second has urethane wheels. As it leans on the same curve, the wheels hold the concrete and the board keeps climbing.

check.q: Who began selling urethane skateboard wheels in the early 1970s?
check.why: Frank Nasworthy sold urethane wheels through his company, Cadillac Wheels.

check.q: Why did urethane wheels work better on a curved wall than clay wheels?
choices: They are harder and more slippery
They grip the concrete with more friction
check.why: Urethane grips better, so the wheels hold when the rider leans on a steep curve.

check.q: What does a bearing do?
choices: holds the grip tape on the deck
connects the trucks to the deck
lets the wheel spin smoothly on the axle
makes the wheel grip the ground
check.why: A bearing is a ring of small steel balls that lets the wheel spin smoothly.

sections.title: Up the Wall and Into the Air

lessons.title: Riding the Curve
lessons.mainIdea: On a curved transition, the wall pushes the skater around the curve, so the skater feels heavier at the bottom.
reading: When a skater rolls into the curve of a pool, their path bends upward. Anything that moves in a curve needs a push toward the center of that curve. Here, the wall gives that push. It presses up on the wheels, which press on the rider's feet. This pull toward the center is called *centripetal acceleration*.

Scientists find centripetal acceleration with a = v squared divided by r. Here v is speed and r is the *radius*, the distance from the center of the curve to the path. Here is a worked example. A skater moves at 6 meters per second through a curve with a 3-meter radius. First, 6 times 6 is 36. Next, 36 divided by 3 is 12. The answer is 12 meters per second squared.

Gravity pulls down at 9.8 meters per second squared. At the bottom of the curve, the floor must hold the rider up and also turn them. So the push adds up to 9.8 plus 12, or 21.8. That is about 2.2 times what the rider feels standing still. This is why pool skaters crouch low with bent knees at the bottom of a wall.

words.d: the change in direction of something moving in a curve, always pointed toward the center of the curve
the distance from the center of a circle or curve to its edge

look.title: Faster Means a Harder Push
look.cite: Worked example using a = v² ÷ r
look.prompt: When the speed doubles from 4 to 8 meters per second, about how many times bigger does the push get?

check.q: What gives a skater the push that turns them around the curve of a pool?
choices: the wall pressing up on the wheels
check.why: The curved wall presses on the wheels and turns the skater's path upward.

check.q: A skater moves at 4 meters per second through a curve with a 2-meter radius. What is the centripetal acceleration?
check.why: 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 divided by 2 is 8 meters per second squared.

check.q: Why do pool skaters crouch at the bottom of a wall?
choices: They feel lighter there and might float
They feel heavier there, and bent knees help them hold it
check.why: At the bottom of the curve the floor pushes harder, so the rider feels heavier and bends to handle it.

lessons.title: Speed From Height
lessons.mainIdea: Starting higher on a wall gives a skater more stored energy, which becomes more speed at the bottom.
reading: A skater at the top of a pool wall is high above the floor. Height stores energy, called *potential energy*. When the skater rolls down, that energy turns into *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion. The higher the start, the faster the skater moves at the bottom. Mass does not change the answer, so a small skater and a large skater reach about the same speed.

If nothing slowed the skater, the speed at the bottom would be v = the square root of 2 times g times h. Here g is 9.8 meters per second squared and h is the height. Here is a worked example for a 2-meter wall. First, 2 times 9.8 is 19.6. Next, 19.6 times 2 is 39.2. The square root of 39.2 is about 6.3. So the speed is about 6.3 meters per second.

Real skaters go a little slower. Friction in the wheels and bearings, and air pushing back, turn some energy into heat and sound. That is why a skater who just rolls back and forth climbs a little lower each time. To keep going, pool skaters learned to pump: crouching on the way into the curve and standing taller on the way up the wall adds energy.

words.d: stored energy that something has because of its height
the energy something has because it is moving
to crouch and stand at the right moments on a ramp to gain speed without pushing

look.title: Wall Height and Speed at the Bottom
look.unit: meters per second, with no friction
look.cite: Worked example using v = √(2gh) with g = 9.8 m/s²
look.prompt: The 4-meter wall is four times as tall as the 1-meter wall. Is the speed four times as fast? About how many times faster is it?

check.q: What kind of energy does a skater have at the top of a pool wall before rolling down?
check.why: Height stores potential energy. It becomes kinetic energy as the skater rolls down.

check.q: With no friction, about how fast is a skater moving after rolling down a 2-meter wall?
check.why: 2 times 9.8 times 2 is 39.2, and its square root is about 6.3 meters per second.

check.q: Why does a skater who only rolls back and forth climb a little lower each time?
choices: Friction and air turn some energy into heat and sound
Kinetic energy turns into more height
check.why: Some energy is lost to friction and air each trip, so the skater cannot reach the starting height.

lessons.title: The Frontside Air
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1970s, pool skaters learned to fly above the coping by grabbing the board, an early trick called the frontside air.
reading: As wheels and walls improved, skaters rode higher and higher. In the late 1970s, some began to fly past the coping and come back down onto the wall. This is called an *air*. To keep the board with them, they grabbed it with one hand. Who did the first one is argued. Tony Alva is often named among the first, and other skaters were trying airs too.

Skaters describe turns as frontside or backside. Skaters call it *frontside* when the skater's chest and toes face the wall as they turn. It is *backside* when their back faces the wall. In a frontside air, the skater rides up the wall facing it, reaches down with the back hand, and grabs the toe-side edge of the board. Then the skater turns in the air and lands going back down the wall.

Physics explains the height. Say a skater leaves the coping moving straight up at 3 meters per second. The rise is v squared divided by 2g. First, 3 times 3 is 9. Next, 2 times 9.8 is 19.6. Then, 9 divided by 19.6 is about 0.46. The skater rises about 0.46 meters above the coping. Airs like this are for experienced riders in a skatepark, after years of smaller steps.

words.d: a trick where the skater and board leave the ramp or wall and fly before landing again
a turn or trick where the skater's chest and toes face the wall or obstacle
a turn or trick where the skater's back faces the wall or obstacle

look.title: A Frontside Air, Frame by Frame
look.text: Frame 1: the skater rolls up the deep-end wall, facing it, knees bent. Frame 2: the wheels reach the coping, and the back hand reaches down to the toe-side edge. Frame 3: skater and board rise together above the coping, turning in the air. Frame 4: the turn finishes, and the wheels meet the wall again, rolling down. Frame 5: the skater crouches low through the transition.
look.prompt: In which frame is the skater moving slowest? Explain using what gravity does on the way up.

check.q: What does frontside mean?
choices: the skater's chest and toes face the wall as they turn
the skater's back faces the wall as they turn
the skater rides with the front foot on the tail
the skater rides in the shallow end
check.why: Frontside means the front of the body faces the wall or obstacle.

check.q: In a frontside air, which hand grabs the board, and where?
choices: the back hand grabs the toe-side edge
the front hand grabs the nose
the back hand grabs the heel-side edge
check.why: In a frontside air the back hand reaches down to the toe-side edge.

check.q: A skater leaves the coping moving straight up at 3 meters per second. About how high above the coping do they rise?
check.why: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 divided by 19.6 is about 0.46 meters.

lessons.title: 1976: Carlsbad and Port Orange
lessons.mainIdea: Two of the first built skateparks, Carlsbad Skatepark in California and Skateboard City in Florida, opened in 1976.
reading: Pools were hard to find, and skating them often meant trespassing. Business owners saw a chance. Why not build places made just for skating? A *skatepark* is a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, bowls and curves. In 1976, two of the first opened on opposite coasts of the United States.

Carlsbad Skatepark opened in Carlsbad, California, north of San Diego. Skateboard City opened in Port Orange, Florida, near Daytona Beach. Both were built of poured concrete. Which one opened first is argued, so it is safest to say both opened in 1976. Florida also had warm weather all year and a strong surfing culture, like California.

Early parks copied what skaters loved about pools. Builders shaped concrete into *bowls*, deep rounded holes with curved walls. Some parks also had snake runs. A snake run is a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks, a bit like a dry riverbed. For the first time, skaters could ride curves legally and without hunting for an empty pool.

words.d: a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, bowls and curves
deep rounded holes in a skatepark with curved walls, shaped like pools
a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks for skating

look.title: From Wheels to Parks
rows: Del Mar Nationals with the Zephyr team
look.cite: Dates as commonly given in skateboarding histories
look.prompt: How many years passed between the kicktail patent and the first parks?

check.q: In what year did Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City both open?
check.why: Both of these early concrete skateparks opened in 1976.

check.q: Where was Skateboard City?
check.why: Skateboard City opened in Port Orange, Florida, near Daytona Beach.

check.q: What is a snake run?
choices: a deep round bowl shaped like a pool
a long, winding downhill channel with curved banks
a wooden ramp in a backyard
check.why: A snake run winds downhill with curved banks, a bit like a dry riverbed.

lessons.title: The Park Boom
lessons.mainIdea: By the late 1970s, dozens of paid skateparks had opened across the United States, often with rules about helmets and pads.
reading: After 1976, skateparks spread quickly. By the late 1970s, dozens had opened across the United States, and parks appeared in other countries too. This fast growth is called a *boom*. It was skateboarding's second boom, after the first one in the early 1960s faded around 1965 and 1966.

Most of these parks were private businesses. Skaters paid to ride, often for a *session*, a set block of time. Many parks had rules that riders wear a helmet and pads. Some rented gear at the front desk. Parks often held contests, and local skaters could watch better riders up close and learn from them.

Parks changed how skaters learned. A beginner could practice on a small, gentle bank before trying a tall bowl. A good progression starts small, with a helmet buckled and pads on, and moves up only when the smaller step feels easy. That idea, start low and build up, began in those first parks and still guides every skatepark today.

words.d: a time of fast growth, when many more people take part and buy products
a set block of time for skating; also a group of skaters riding together
learning in steps, from easy and low to harder and higher

look.title: A Day at a 1970s Park
look.text: A skater pays at a window and gets a wristband for a two-hour session. A sign says helmets and pads are required. Inside, a small bank sits near the entrance, a snake run winds downhill, and a deep bowl waits at the back. Beginners practice turns on the bank. Older riders carve the bowl, and a crowd gathers at its edge to watch.
look.prompt: Where in this park would you start, and what would make you ready to move to the next area?

check.q: What was a session at a 1970s skatepark?
choices: a set block of time that skaters paid to ride
a kind of trick in the air
the deepest bowl in the park
check.why: Many parks charged skaters for a session, a set block of time.

check.q: Which boom was the skatepark boom of the late 1970s?
check.why: The first boom faded around 1965 and 1966. The park boom of the 1970s was the second.

check.q: What does a good progression look like?
choices: start in the deepest bowl to learn fast
skip the helmet on small banks
start low and small with gear, and move up when that step feels easy
check.why: A progression builds from easy and low to harder and higher, with gear on.

lessons.title: SkateBoarder Magazine
lessons.mainIdea: SkateBoarder magazine spread pool and park skating across the country through photos and stories in the 1970s.
reading: Before the internet, most skaters learned about new tricks from *magazines*. The most important one in the 1970s was SkateBoarder. It first appeared in the 1960s, stopped when the first boom faded, and came back in the mid-1970s. Each issue had big color photos of skaters in pools and parks.

Photos showed what words could not. A picture of a skater high on a pool wall told a kid in another state that it could be done. Writer and artist Craig Stecyk wrote about the Santa Monica and Venice skaters, an area called *Dogtown*. Those stories helped make Zephyr riders famous far from California.

Magazines also ran ads for boards, wheels and parks. Companies paid skaters to ride their products. These skaters were called *pros*, short for professionals. A young skater who wanted to see the newest tricks waited each month for the next issue to arrive.

words.d: printed publications with photos and stories that come out on a schedule, such as every month
a nickname for parts of Santa Monica and Venice, California, where the Zephyr skaters rode
short for professionals; skaters paid to ride for a company

look.title: A Photo Travels
look.text: A photographer kneels at the edge of a deep pool in California. Click: a skater hangs at the top of the wall, wheels just below the tile. Weeks later, that photo is printed across two pages of a magazine. A kid far from the coast opens the magazine and stares at it for a long time. The next day, the kid draws a pool wall in a notebook.
look.prompt: How did one photo change what a skater far away believed was possible?

check.q: What was the most important skateboarding magazine of the 1970s?
check.why: SkateBoarder led in the 1970s. Thrasher began in 1981 and TransWorld in 1983.

check.q: What was Dogtown?
choices: a nickname for parts of Santa Monica and Venice where the Zephyr skaters rode
check.why: Dogtown was a nickname for an area of Santa Monica and Venice, written about by Craig Stecyk.

check.q: What is a pro skater?
choices: a skater paid to ride for a company
a skater who only rides pools
check.why: Pro is short for professional, a skater who is paid to ride a company's products.

lessons.title: Insurance and Lawsuits
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1980s, high insurance costs and injury lawsuits closed many skateparks.
reading: Skaters fall, and sometimes they get hurt. When someone was hurt at a park, they or their family could sue the owner. A *lawsuit* is a case taken to court to ask for money for a harm. Even a park that won in court had to pay lawyers. Each lawsuit raised the risk of running a park.

Park owners bought *insurance*. Insurance is a plan where you pay a company regularly, and it pays big costs if something goes wrong. As claims grew, insurance companies charged park owners more, or refused to cover them. For many owners, the cost became more than the park earned.

Many parks closed in the early 1980s. Some were torn down. Others were filled with dirt and buried. At the same time, fewer people were buying skateboards, so parks had fewer paying riders. Losing the parks was a blow, but skaters did not stop. They found other places to ride.

words.d: a case taken to court in which someone asks for money for a harm
a plan where you pay a company regularly and it pays large costs if something goes wrong

look.title: A Park Owner's Math
look.text: Picture the money for one park as two piles. Pile one is money coming in: session fees, gear rentals and snacks. Pile two is money going out: workers, repairs, electric bills and insurance. One year the insurance bill doubles. Pile two grows taller than pile one. Then fewer skaters come, and pile one shrinks.
look.prompt: What choices does the owner have when the money going out is bigger than the money coming in?

check.q: What closed many skateparks in the early 1980s?
choices: the start of the X Games
high insurance costs and injury lawsuits
check.why: Rising insurance costs and lawsuits made many parks too expensive to run.

check.q: What is insurance?
choices: a rule that skaters must wear pads
a plan where you pay a company and it pays big costs if something goes wrong
check.why: Insurance spreads risk: you pay regularly, and the company pays large costs.

check.q: Besides insurance, what else made parks harder to keep open?
choices: fewer people were buying skateboards, so fewer riders came

lessons.title: What Skaters Did Next
lessons.mainIdea: When parks closed, skaters built wooden ramps and took to the streets, and later public parks returned.
reading: With parks closing, skaters built their own places. Many built *halfpipes* out of wood in backyards. A halfpipe is a U-shaped ramp with two curved walls facing each other. Plywood bent over wooden frames made a smooth transition. Friends pooled money for lumber and built them together.

Other skaters rode what the city already had: curbs, banks, benches and empty parking lots. This became *street skating*, which grew in the 1980s. It needed new tricks, and the ollie on flat ground would soon give skaters a way to get up onto things without ramps.

Skateparks came back, but in a new form. Over time, more cities built *public* parks, owned by the town and often free to use. Some states changed their laws to protect cities from many lawsuits when skaters at public parks are hurt. Today a good first visit still means a helmet that fits and is buckled, wrist guards and pads, and starting on the smallest bank.

skating on things found in a town, such as curbs, ledges and banks
owned by a town or city and open to everyone

chapters.title: The Ollie and the Street
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one no-hands trick change where and how people skate?

story.title: No Hands
story.kicker: At a Florida skatepark in the late 1970s, a board leaps into the air and nobody is holding it.
paragraphs: It is the late 1970s at a concrete skatepark in Florida. A young skater sits on the edge of a bowl, watching. Every rider who flies above the coping does the same thing. They reach down, grab the board with one hand, and hold it so it does not fall away. Everyone thinks that is the only way to get air.

Then an older rider drops into the bowl. He carves fast across the bottom and rolls up the far wall. Near the top, his back foot stamps down on the tail. The board pops up off the wall. His hands stay out by his sides, not on the board. For a moment, rider and board hang above the coping together.

The young skater leans forward. How is the board staying under his feet? Nothing is holding it. The rider turns in the air and comes back down onto the wall, wheels first, and rolls away. Someone at the edge shouts. Another skater tries it on the next run and the board shoots off on its own.

Riders in Florida were trying this trick in the late 1970s. One of them, Alan Gelfand, had the nickname Ollie, and the trick took his name. Within a few years, a teenager named Rodney Mullen would do it on flat ground. Once a board could jump with no hands and no ramp, the whole city became a place to skate.
story.think: Why would a trick with no hands be harder to believe than a trick where the skater grabs the board?

lessons.title: Alan Gelfand's No-Hands Air
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1970s, Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand popped his board into the air on a ramp wall with no hands, and the ollie was named for him.
reading: Alan Gelfand skated in Florida in the late 1970s. His friends called him Ollie. He found that he could pop his board into the air at the top of a transition without grabbing it. At the top of the wall, he stamped hard on the *tail*, the back end of the board that bends upward. The board lifted, and he lifted with it.

Other skaters called the trick the *ollie* air, and later just the ollie. An ollie is a jump where the skater pops the tail and the board rises with their feet, with no hands. At first, the ollie was done only on ramps and in bowls. Many skaters saw it in magazine photos before they ever saw it in person.

The ollie depended on an older idea: the *kicktail*. That is the upturned tail of a board. Larry Stevenson's patent for a kicktail was granted in 1971. Without a tail to push on, there is nothing for the back foot to snap. The kicktail made the kickturn possible, and later it made the ollie possible.

words.d: the back end of a skateboard deck, usually bent upward
a jump where the skater pops the tail and the board rises with the feet, with no hands
an upturned tail on a skateboard deck; Larry Stevenson's patent for it was granted in 1971

look.title: Grab Air or No-Hands Air
look.text: Picture two riders at the top of the same bowl. The first reaches down and grabs the edge of the board, holding it to their feet as they fly over the coping. The second keeps both arms out. At the lip, the back foot stamps on the tail, and the board jumps up with the rider's feet. Both come back down onto the wall.
look.prompt: What part of the board does the second rider use instead of a hand to keep the board close?

check.why: Alan Gelfand's nickname was Ollie, and the trick was named for him.

check.q: Where was the ollie first done?
check.why: Gelfand's ollie was a no-hands air at the top of a transition. Flat ground came later.

check.q: Why did the ollie depend on the kicktail?
choices: The kicktail makes the wheels grip
The kicktail keeps the board from turning
The back foot needs a tail to snap down on
check.why: An ollie starts with the back foot snapping the tail, so the board needs a kicktail.

lessons.title: How a Board Pops Up
lessons.mainIdea: In an ollie, the back foot snaps the tail, the ground pushes back, the board tips up on its back wheels, and the front foot drags it level.
reading: An ollie is a chain of forces. First, the back foot snaps the tail down hard. The tail hits the ground. By *Newton's third law*, when one thing pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction. So the ground pushes up on the tail, and the board starts to rise.

The board also acts as a *lever*. A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a point called a pivot. Here the pivot is the back wheels. When the tail goes down, the nose swings up. The turning effect is called *torque*, found by force times the distance from the pivot. Here is a worked example. A back foot pushes with 500 newtons, 0.15 meters from the back wheels. 500 times 0.15 is 75, so the torque is 75 newton-meters.

Now the board is tilted, nose high. The front foot slides up toward the nose. Grip tape is rough, so friction lets the shoe drag the board upward. The front foot then pushes the nose forward and down until the board is level. The rider jumps at the same time and pulls the knees up, so the board has room to rise.

words.d: when one thing pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction
a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point called a pivot
the turning effect of a force, found by force times the distance from the pivot

look.title: A Ruler and a Board
look.text: Lay a ruler on a desk so one end sticks out past the edge. Tap the end that sticks out. The ruler turns at the desk edge, and the far end lifts. Now picture a skateboard. The back wheels are the desk edge. The tail is the end you tap. When the tail is struck, the nose lifts. The longer the distance from pivot to foot, the bigger the turn for the same push.
look.prompt: On a skateboard, what plays the part of the desk edge? What plays the part of your tapping finger?

check.q: When the tail hits the ground in an ollie, what pushes the board up?
choices: the ground pushing back on the tail
check.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back up on the tail as hard as the tail hits it.

check.q: In an ollie, what is the pivot of the lever?
check.why: The board turns around the back wheels, so the nose rises when the tail goes down.

check.q: A foot pushes with 400 newtons, 0.15 meters from the pivot. What is the torque?
check.why: 400 times 0.15 is 60 newton-meters.

lessons.title: How Long an Ollie Lasts
lessons.mainIdea: Hang time depends on how high the rider rises; a 30-centimeter ollie keeps a rider in the air about half a second.
reading: Once a skater leaves the ground, gravity takes over. The skater rises, slows, stops at the top, and falls back. The time from takeoff to landing is called *hang time*. The path of the skater's middle traces a smooth arch called a *parabola*. A higher jump means a longer hang time.

There is a formula for hang time. If h is the jump height, the time is 2 times the square root of 2h divided by g. Here is a worked example for a 0.30-meter ollie. First, 2 times 0.30 is 0.60. Next, 0.60 divided by 9.8 is about 0.061. The square root of 0.061 is about 0.247. Last, 2 times 0.247 is about 0.49. The rider is in the air about half a second.

Half a second is very short. In that time the front foot has to drag the board level and both feet have to come back over the bolts. That is why skaters practice the same motion many times. The landing matters too. Bending the knees on landing spreads the stop over more time, which makes the force on the legs smaller.

words.d: the time a skater spends in the air, from takeoff to landing
the smooth arch-shaped path of something thrown or jumping through the air

look.title: Ollie Height and Hang Time
look.cite: Worked example using t = 2√(2h/g) with g = 9.8 m/s²
look.prompt: The 0.40-meter ollie is twice as high as the 0.20-meter ollie. Is its hang time twice as long?

check.q: What is hang time?
choices: the time a skater spends in the air
the time it takes to push off
check.why: Hang time runs from takeoff to landing.

check.q: About how long is a rider in the air during a 0.30-meter ollie?
check.why: 2 times the square root of 0.60 divided by 9.8 is about 0.49 seconds.

check.q: Why do skaters bend their knees when they land?
choices: It makes the board fly higher
It spreads the stop over more time, so the force is smaller
check.why: Stopping over a longer time means a smaller force on the legs.

lessons.title: Freestyle Skating
lessons.mainIdea: Freestyle was a style of flat-ground skating done as a routine, and Rodney Mullen became its best-known rider.
reading: In the 1970s and 1980s, one kind of contest needed no ramp at all. It was called *freestyle*. Freestyle skaters did tricks on smooth flat ground, one after another, in a routine set to music. They spun on the back wheels, stood the board on its end, and flipped it with their feet. Judges scored the whole routine.

Rodney Mullen grew up in Florida. As a teenager he won freestyle contests again and again, and he kept inventing new tricks. He rode for Powell Peralta, one of the biggest skateboard companies of the 1980s. Freestyle taught him to control a board with tiny movements of his feet.

Freestyle boards were often smaller and lighter than ramp boards. They had a tail and a nose to stand on and spin. Freestyle contests faded by the end of the 1980s, but the control they built did not. Many of today's flat-ground tricks began as freestyle tricks.

words.d: a style of skating on flat ground, with tricks done one after another in a routine
a planned set of tricks done in order, often to music, for judges

look.title: A Freestyle Routine
look.text: A skater stands on a smooth, flat floor. Music starts. They roll forward and spin around on the back wheels three times. They step off, flip the board onto its side with one foot, and balance on its edge. Then they flick it back onto its wheels and roll into the next trick. There is no ramp, no rail and no curb, only a board and feet.
look.prompt: What skill would a freestyle routine build that would help with every other kind of skating?

check.q: What was freestyle skating?
choices: a routine of tricks on flat ground, often to music
check.why: Freestyle skaters did tricks one after another on flat ground, often to music.

check.q: Which company did Rodney Mullen ride for in the 1980s?
check.why: Mullen rode for Powell Peralta, one of the largest companies of the 1980s.

check.q: What did freestyle teach Rodney Mullen?
choices: to control the board with tiny movements of his feet
to grab the board in the air
check.why: Freestyle depends on small, precise foot movements on flat ground.

lessons.title: The Ollie on Flat Ground
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1980s, Rodney Mullen did the ollie on flat ground, so a skater could jump with no ramp at all.
reading: Gelfand's ollie happened at the top of a ramp wall. In the early 1980s, Rodney Mullen found a way to do it on *flat ground*, meaning level pavement with no ramp. He snapped the tail, slid his front foot up, and the board rose off the floor with his feet. Skaters had never seen a board jump from flat ground with no hands.

This changed what a skater could do. With a flat-ground ollie, a skater could hop up onto a curb, over a crack or onto a low ledge without stopping. It turned the whole street into terrain. In skating, *terrain* is any surface or object a skater rides, from a bowl wall to a curb.

Learning it still takes many steps. First, a skater practices standing still on grass or carpet, where the board cannot roll away. Next, they try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground with a helmet buckled and pads on. Only after many clean landings do they try to ollie up onto something low, such as a painted curb.

words.d: level pavement with no ramp
any surface or object a skater rides, such as a bowl, a bank or a curb

look.title: One Curb, Two Skaters
look.text: Two skaters roll toward the same low curb. The first has no ollie. They stop, pick up the board, step up and start again. The second crouches as they roll, snaps the tail, slides the front foot, and the board hops up onto the curb with their feet on it. They keep rolling without stopping.
look.prompt: List three other things in a town that the second skater could now ride that the first could not.

check.q: What did Rodney Mullen do with the ollie in the early 1980s?
choices: He did it on flat ground with no ramp
He did it only on vert ramps
He made the first urethane wheel
check.why: Mullen brought the ollie from ramps to flat ground in the early 1980s.

check.q: Why did the flat-ground ollie change street skating?
choices: It ended freestyle the next day
It let skaters ride without wheels
Skaters could hop onto curbs and ledges without stopping
check.why: A board that jumps from flat ground can get onto curbs and ledges in a town.

choices: try it rolling fast down a hill
try it onto a high ledge
practice standing still on grass or carpet
try it at the top of a ramp
check.why: Grass or carpet keeps the board from rolling while the motion is learned.

lessons.title: Kickflips and Flip Tricks
lessons.mainIdea: Rodney Mullen invented the kickflip as it is done today, along with other flip tricks like the heelflip and the 360 flip.
reading: Once the board could jump from flat ground, Mullen began to spin and flip it in the air. His best-known invention is the *kickflip* as skaters do it today. In a kickflip, the skater ollies, and the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose. The board flips over along its long side, then the feet catch it and land.

Skaters had flipped boards in other ways before, but Mullen's version starts from an ollie. He also invented the *heelflip*. In a heelflip, the front foot flicks off the heel-side edge with the heel, and the board flips the other way. Mixing a flip with a spin led to the 360 flip, also credited to Mullen.

A flip trick is called a *flip trick* because the board turns over under the skater. These tricks look like magic, but they follow the same rules as the ollie. They are learned after a steady rolling ollie, first by practicing the flick standing still on grass. Landing with both feet over the bolts is the goal every time.

words.d: an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose so the board flips along its long side
an ollie in which the front heel flicks off the heel-side edge so the board flips the opposite way from a kickflip
a trick where the board turns over under the skater in the air

look.title: Kickflip and Heelflip Side by Side
look.text: Two skaters ollie at the same moment. The first slides the front foot up and flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose with the side of the shoe. The board rolls over along its long side. The second slides the front foot up and pushes the heel off the heel-side edge. That board rolls over along its long side too, but in the opposite direction. Both boards land wheels down, and both skaters catch with their feet.
look.prompt: Which edge does the front foot leave in each trick? Say it with toe side and heel side.

check.q: In a kickflip, how does the front foot flip the board?
choices: It flicks off the heel-side edge with the heel
It kicks the tail down only
It flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose
It grabs the board by hand
check.why: In a kickflip the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge. The heelflip uses the heel side.

check.q: How is a heelflip different from a kickflip?
choices: The back foot flips it instead of the front foot
The heel flicks the heel-side edge, and the board flips the other way
The board spins flat instead of flipping
check.why: A heelflip uses the heel on the heel-side edge, so the board turns the opposite way.

check.q: When should a skater start learning flip tricks?
choices: after a steady rolling ollie, starting standing still on grass
on the first day, rolling fast
check.why: Flip tricks build on the ollie, and the flick is first practiced standing still.

lessons.title: The Bones Brigade
lessons.mainIdea: Powell Peralta's team, the Bones Brigade, gathered young riders such as Tony Hawk and Rodney Mullen in the 1980s.
reading: Powell Peralta was a skateboard company run by George Powell and Stacy Peralta. Peralta had skated with the Zephyr team in the 1970s. In the 1980s he built a team of young riders called the *Bones Brigade*. A skate *team* is a group of skaters a company sponsors to ride its products in contests, photos and videos.

The Bones Brigade included Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, Mike McGill, Lance Mountain, Tommy Guerrero and Rodney Mullen. Some rode vert ramps, some rode street and one rode freestyle. Tony Hawk joined as a young teenager and became one of the best-known skaters in the world.

The company's boards had bold *graphics*, the pictures printed on the bottom of a deck. Artist Vernon Courtland Johnson drew many of them, often with skulls and bones. Kids could spot a Powell Peralta board across a parking lot. A board's art became a way for a skater to show who they were.

words.d: Powell Peralta's 1980s team of skaters, including Tony Hawk and Rodney Mullen
a group of skaters a company sponsors to ride its products
the pictures printed on the bottom of a skateboard deck

look.title: One Team, Many Styles
look.text: Picture the Bones Brigade lined up for a photo. One rider carries a wide vert board for tall ramps. Another holds a board scuffed from curbs and city streets. A third holds a small, light freestyle board. Each board has a bold picture on the bottom. They ride different terrain, but they wear the same team name.
look.prompt: Why might a company want riders who skate different kinds of terrain on one team?

check.q: Who ran the Powell Peralta company?
check.why: George Powell and Stacy Peralta ran Powell Peralta.

check.q: Which skater was a member of the Bones Brigade?
check.why: Tony Hawk joined the Bones Brigade as a young teenager.

the pictures printed on the bottom of the deck

lessons.title: Skate Videos on Tape
lessons.mainIdea: The Bones Brigade Video Show of 1984 showed skaters that tricks could be learned by watching moving pictures at home.
reading: In 1984, Powell Peralta released The Bones Brigade Video Show. It was a skate *video*, a film of skaters doing tricks, sold on tape. Families could play it at home on a VCR, a machine that played video tapes. Skaters watched it over and over.

A photo shows one frozen moment. A video shows the whole trick: the crouch, the pop, the landing. Skaters could pause, rewind and watch the feet. Powell Peralta made more videos, including Future Primitive in 1985 and The Search for Animal Chin in 1987. Videos became one of the main ways tricks spread.

Videos also made skaters famous in towns with no skatepark. A kid in a small town could study the best riders in the world without leaving home. Copies were passed from friend to friend. Later, in the 1990s, videos from many companies would take over this job.

words.d: a recorded film of moving pictures, such as a film of skaters doing tricks
a video cassette recorder; a machine that played video tapes on a TV

look.title: Magazines and Videos of the 1980s
look.cite: Publication and release years as commonly given in skateboarding histories

check.q: In what year was The Bones Brigade Video Show released?
check.why: Powell Peralta released The Bones Brigade Video Show in 1984.

choices: the whole trick from crouch to landing
check.why: A video shows every step of a trick in motion, and it can be paused and rewound.

check.q: What was a VCR?
choices: a machine that played video tapes on a TV
check.why: A VCR, or video cassette recorder, played tapes like The Bones Brigade Video Show.

lessons.title: Thrasher and TransWorld
lessons.mainIdea: Two magazines that started in the early 1980s, Thrasher (1981) and TransWorld SKATEboarding (1983), kept skating connected after parks closed.
reading: When parks closed and sales fell in the early 1980s, skaters needed ways to stay connected. Two new magazines filled that need. Thrasher began in 1981 in San Francisco. TransWorld SKATEboarding began in 1983. Both covered vert ramps, backyard ramps and the new street skating.

Each *issue*, one printing of a magazine, carried photos, interviews and contest results. Many issues also printed *sequence* photos. A sequence is a row of photos taken quickly, one after another, showing each step of a trick. A skater could study a sequence like a set of instructions.

Magazines linked skaters in different places. A reader in Illinois could see what was happening in California or Florida that month. Ads listed skate shops and mail-order catalogs. For many skaters in the 1980s, the magazine and the video were the closest thing to a skatepark.

words.d: one printing of a magazine, such as the March issue
a row of photos taken quickly, one after another, showing each step of a trick

look.title: Reading a Sequence
look.text: Picture six small photos in a row across a page. Photo 1: the skater rolls, knees bent. Photo 2: the tail hits the ground. Photo 3: the front foot slides up and the nose rises. Photo 4: the board is level, high under the knees. Photo 5: the board drops back toward the ground. Photo 6: the wheels touch down and the knees bend.
look.prompt: Which photo shows the moment the ground pushes back on the tail? Which shows the board being leveled?

check.q: In what year did Thrasher magazine begin?
check.why: Thrasher began in 1981 in San Francisco. TransWorld SKATEboarding began in 1983.

check.q: What is a sequence in a skate magazine?
choices: an ad for a skate shop
a row of quick photos showing each step of a trick
check.why: A sequence shows a trick step by step in photos taken one after another.

check.q: Why were magazines so important to skaters in the early 1980s?
choices: They were the only place to buy wheels
Parks had closed, and magazines kept skaters in different places connected
check.why: With parks closing, magazines carried tricks, news and photos to skaters everywhere.

lessons.title: Backyard Ramps
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1980s, skaters built wooden halfpipes in backyards, and small mini ramps became a common place to learn.
reading: With concrete parks closing, skaters turned to wood. Friends and families built halfpipes in backyards and driveways. The frame was made of wooden ribs cut into a curve. Sheets of plywood were bent over the ribs to make a smooth transition. A metal pipe along the top edge served as coping.

Tall ramps with vert walls were used for big airs and contests. Many backyards had a *mini ramp* instead, a smaller halfpipe with no vertical part. On a mini ramp, a skater can learn to pump, kickturn and roll back and forth at low speed. At the top of each wall is the *platform*, a flat deck where skaters stand and wait their turn.

A safe ramp starts with a strong frame and smooth, tight plywood with no gaps or loose screws. Adults with building experience did, and still should, lead the work. Riders on any ramp wear a buckled helmet and pads. Taking turns on the platform keeps two skaters from crashing at the bottom.

words.d: a small halfpipe with curved walls but no vertical part
the flat area at the top of a ramp wall where skaters stand and wait

look.title: Building a Mini Ramp
look.text: Picture a mini ramp from the side. Two curved walls face each other with a short flat bottom between them. Each wall is made of wooden ribs, all cut to the same curve and lined up in a row. Plywood is bent across the ribs and screwed down flat. A round metal pipe runs along each top edge. Behind each pipe is a flat platform where a skater stands with a foot on the tail.
look.prompt: Why must all the ribs be cut to the same curve? What would happen to the board if one rib were too short?

check.q: What is a mini ramp?
choices: a ramp made of concrete in a park
a small halfpipe with no vertical part
a single curb in a parking lot
a tall vert ramp for contests
check.why: A mini ramp is a smaller halfpipe without vert walls.

check.q: What did skaters use as coping on wooden ramps?
choices: a metal pipe along the top edge
check.why: Wooden ramps used a metal pipe along the top edge as coping.

check.q: Why do skaters take turns from the platform?
choices: It is the only way to pump
It keeps two skaters from crashing at the bottom
check.why: One rider at a time keeps skaters from running into each other.

lessons.title: Curbs, Ledges and the Street
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1980s, street skaters used the ollie to ride curbs, ledges and banks, starting with low objects first.
reading: By the mid-1980s, the ollie had opened up the street. Skaters such as Mark Gonzales and Natas Kaupas showed new ways to ride things found in towns. A curb could be ollied onto. A *ledge*, a long low block like the edge of a planter, could be ground along. A *bank*, a slanted wall of concrete, worked like a small ramp.

Street skating used what was already there, so anyone with a board could try it. Some skaters in videos also jumped down stairs and rode handrails. Those were advanced feats done by experienced riders, not things to try while learning. Many skaters also met trouble from guards and police, because skating in some public places was banned.

A safe way to start street skating is at a skatepark's street section or on a painted curb in an empty lot, away from cars. First, practice the ollie rolling on flat ground. Next, ollie onto a curb only a few centimeters high. Then add a little height when landing feels easy. A buckled helmet and wrist guards go on every time.

words.d: a long, low block, like the edge of a planter or bench, that skaters ride along
a slanted wall of concrete that works like a small ramp

look.title: From Flat to Curb
look.text: Step 1: on grass, the skater practices the ollie motion standing still. Step 2: on smooth pavement, they ollie while rolling slowly and land on the bolts. Step 3: they ollie over a line drawn in chalk. Step 4: they ollie onto a low painted curb at a skatepark. Each step repeats until it feels easy before the next one begins.
look.prompt: Why does each step add just one new challenge? Which step would you practice longest?

check.q: Which skaters showed new ways to ride the street in the mid-1980s?
check.why: Mark Gonzales and Natas Kaupas helped shape street skating in the mid-1980s.

check.q: What is a bank?
choices: a long low block like a planter edge
a metal pipe on a ramp
a slanted wall of concrete that works like a small ramp
the flat top of a ramp
check.why: A bank is a slanted concrete wall. A ledge is a long low block.

check.q: What is a safe first object to ollie onto?
choices: a low painted curb at a skatepark
a curb next to busy traffic
check.why: Start low and away from cars, such as a painted curb only a few centimeters high.

review.q: Who was the ollie named for?
choices: Alan Gelfand, whose nickname was Ollie
review.why: Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand did the no-hands air on ramps in the late 1970s.

review.q: What did Rodney Mullen add to the ollie in the early 1980s?
choices: He made it a contest rule
He did it on flat ground
review.why: Mullen brought the ollie to flat ground, which opened up street skating.

review.q: Which order matches the start of an ollie?
choices: jump, crouch, slide the back foot, snap the nose
slide the front foot, crouch, land, snap the tail
snap the nose, jump, crouch, land
crouch, snap the tail, slide the front foot, jump
review.why: An ollie starts with a crouch, then the tail snap, the front foot slide and the jump.

review.q: In a kickflip, which part of the shoe flicks the board, and off which edge?
choices: the back foot, off the heel-side edge of the tail
the front heel, off the heel-side edge
the front foot, off the toe-side edge of the nose
the back foot, straight down on the tail only
review.why: The kickflip's flick comes from the front foot off the toe-side edge.

review.q: About how long is a skater in the air during a 0.30-meter ollie?
review.why: Using t = 2 times the square root of 2h divided by g gives about 0.49 seconds.

review.q: What did The Bones Brigade Video Show (1984) let skaters do?
choices: watch whole tricks at home and replay them
skate in a new public park
review.why: On tape, skaters could pause and rewind to study each trick.

review.q: Which two magazines began in the early 1980s?
review.why: Thrasher began in 1981 and TransWorld SKATEboarding in 1983.

review.q: Why did many skaters build wooden ramps in the 1980s?
choices: Pools were all full of water
review.why: When parks closed over insurance costs, skaters built their own halfpipes.
